title: WISER: Systematic Design-Space Exploration of Fault-Tolerant Global Control Trapped-Ions
authors: Scott Jones, Song-qing-hao Yang, Prakash Murali
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers are a leading candidate for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing, but conventional Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architectures face severe wiring and power constraints as systems scale. The recently proposed WISE promise orders-of-magnitude reductions in wiring complexity but fundamentally alter the hardware--software interface, making it unclear whether such restrictive architectures can feasibly execute quantum error correction (QEC) and eventually support fault-tolerant workloads. We present WISER, a cross-layer architectural design-space exploration framework for globally controlled trapped-ion systems, to determine whether WISE can support early FTQC, and what hardware/compiler/QEC choices are needed. WISER combines novel WISE-specific compilation, noise modelling, and simulation and integrated them into a unified framework. WISER provides comparative lower-bound estimates of logical clock speed and logical error rate, rather than absolute hardware prediction, enabling us to identify viable operating regions while ruling out infeasible ones. To our knowledge, it is the first systematic design space exploration study targeted at WISE and scalable architectures beyond QCCD. Using WISER, we identify a narrow feasible design space requiring two-ion traps, moderate control multiplexing, aggressive recooling, and high-rate bivariate-bicycle codes. Even under $\sim 10\times$ improvements in physical errors, the lower-bound cycle time to achieve $< 10^{-8}$ logical error is $\approx 100\,ms$, which is $3\times$ slower than local control. These results expose a fundamental trade-off between wiring scalability and logical throughput, suggesting that practical early fault-tolerant operation requires complementary $> 10\times$ physical error rate reductions along with substantial $> 100\times$ reduction in fault-tolerant circuit-depth.
summary: This paper introduces WISER, a comprehensive framework to systematically explore the design space for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing using the advanced WISE architecture. By integrating compilation, noise modeling, and simulation, the authors determine that while WISE offers wiring advantages, achieving high logical throughput requires substantial, complementary improvements in both physical error rates and circuit depth. This work highlights a critical trade-off between hardware scalability and computational performance.
main_problem: The paper addresses the feasibility of implementing fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) on trapped-ion systems using the novel, wiring-constrained WISE architecture.
main_result: The study identifies a narrow feasible design space requiring specific hardware choices (two-ion traps, moderate multiplexing) and warns of a fundamental trade-off between wiring scalability and logical throughput.
method: A cross-layer architectural design-space exploration framework (WISER) was developed, combining novel compilation, detailed noise modeling, and simulation to estimate logical performance metrics.
model_or_system: The system is trapped-ion quantum computing, comparing the conventional QCCD architecture against the highly scalable, but restrictive, WISE architecture. The analysis incorporates detailed noise models for electric field fluctuations, heating, and crosstalk.
key_observables: Logical clock speed, logical error rate ($p_L$), and the required cycle time to achieve target error thresholds (e.g., $< 10^{-8}$).
important_parameters: Multiplexing order ($M$), trap capacity ($k$), physical error rates, and the required reduction factors for circuit depth and physical errors ($> 10	imes$ and $> 100	imes$, respectively).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the QEC specification can be mapped to a noiseless circuit before being lowered to the WISE gate set, and it models noise sources like phonon accumulation and correlated crosstalk.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the WISER workflow (QEC Spec $ightarrow$ Compilation $ightarrow$ Simulation), show convergence traces for SAT-based optimization (e.g., Steane code), and detail the physical layout and noise sources.
paper_structure: The paper is structured around the WISER framework, detailing the compilation process, the integration of noise models (including electric field noise and crosstalk), and finally, using SAT solvers to systematically explore the design space and determine performance bounds.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, systematic, and hardware-aware methodology for assessing the scalability limits of next-generation quantum hardware, which is crucial for theoretical work aiming to bridge abstract quantum codes to physical implementation.

Figure 1. Overview of WISER (★= new tool contributions). A QEC code and a WISE configuration are fed as inputs. Output includes logical error rate 𝑝𝐿and QEC cycle time. The QEC spec is first converted to an architecture-agnostic, noiseless Stim circuit. Then it is lowered to the gate set supported by WISE and mapped and scheduled on the architecture. Following this, a WISE noise model-specific Stim simulation is run to determine QEC parameters. Changing chip parameters requires recompilation through the red dashed box; changing control parameters requires re-simulation through the dotted box, bypassing the SAT solver.
